sourceBindings.text: Like a mechanic reading diagnostic results before proposing a repair, a soil technician investigates before suggesting a field input. Guessing can waste money, injure a crop and create pollution. This step brings together safe sample handling, pH and texture measurements, and supplied nutrient and organic-matter results; a report alone does not prove that its writer performed every test. What other professions use diagnostic tests before deciding what to do, such as doctors or computer technicians? Why is guessing a poor approach?

The 95-minute active lesson plan allocates 5 minutes to introduction/outcomes, 35 to instruction, 10 to interpretation/report discussion and 45 to activity/discussion. Sample drying, full jar settling and laboratory turnaround require additional elapsed time. A trainer may stage the work and assess the learner's own actions at each stage.

sourceBindings.text: Put on the required PPE, check the prepared Field 3 sample, its ID and date, and record whether drying and sieving were already completed. A prepared sample is not evidence that you dried it. Measure pH with the actual instrument and approved method, and determine texture from your own staged jar or validated texture method; retain raw observations and conditions.

The trainer supplies Field 3 organic matter 2.1%, phosphorus 12 ppm and potassium 185 ppm after the learner's physical work. The nutrient extract–react–read-color sequence is taught conceptually; the trainer demonstrates organic-matter testing. Understand and interpret these results, but do not claim that you independently ran NPK or organic-matter laboratory assays. Nitrogen has no supplied Field 3 number, so leave it unmeasured.

sourceBindings.text: The classroom chart gives pH low <6.0, example optimum 6.0–7.5 and high >7.5; OM low <2%, optimum 3–6%, high >6%; P low <15 ppm, optimum 20–40 ppm, high >50 ppm; K low <100 ppm, optimum 120–200 ppm, high >250 ppm; and an N example low <10 ppm while other N classes vary. These are the chart's illustrative figures, not universal crop thresholds. Its OM 2–3%, P 15–20 and 40–50 ppm, and K 100–120 and 200–250 ppm intervals and some exact boundaries are not classified by that chart. State a gap; do not silently bridge it.

The same chart offers lime for low pH, sulfur or acidifying fertilizer for high pH, compost/manure/cover crops for low OM, MAP or DAP for low P, potash for low K and withholding extra P or K when high. Preserve these as discussion examples only. Any material, need and rate require suitable crop, laboratory and site evidence; sulfur especially needs a compatible soil and a locally justified plan. Its statement that a low N snapshot confirms application is too strong without the crop nitrogen budget.

Use the testing laboratory's extraction and measurement methods, units, crop-specific interpretation and regional guidance. Phosphorus 12 ppm, for example, can have different meaning under Bray and Olsen extraction. A single soil nitrogen number is a time-specific clue; crop requirement, prior inputs, nitrogen credits and timing matter. The classroom N meal and P/K pantry analogy helps remember this difference but cannot set a rate.

sourceBindings.text: Include client, field and sample IDs, collection/test dates, crop and location. In a results table, put each parameter, measured value and unit, method, data origin, interpretation reference and status. List texture percentages and class from the learner's record; pH is unitless; OM is a percentage; P and K are reported in ppm in this exercise. Mark any missing method or result as missing, not zero.

Explain each conclusion and what further evidence is needed. Recommendations must be specific enough to guide the next diagnostic or management decision, yet no numeric application rate is justified by this incomplete classroom report. The sample text's [X] lime and [Y] MAP (11-52-0) are placeholders, and a product label is not a crop-specific dose. Record observations, limitations and the trainer's review separately.

A separate maize report-template example uses pH 5.8 and an illustrative target 6.5, with [X amount] of agricultural lime per acre; its phosphorus template uses [Y amount] of MAP(11-52-0). This demonstrates report structure, not a measured Field 3 result or a justified rate. Keep the placeholders unresolved until the crop target, lime requirement and calibrated nutrient plan are supplied. Its comments example links sandy texture to a possible need for more frequent irrigation; verify the crop, rooting depth, weather and actual water status before changing a schedule.

sourceBindings.text: For the source's 40-minute practical block and 5-minute discussion, Part 1 is a proposed 20 minutes for PPE, sample inspection, learner pH and texture setup; Part 2 proposes 20 minutes for receiving supplied OM/P/K data, interpretation and report writing. The trainer releases the supplied data after physical measurements. The source acknowledges roughly 24 hours for full jar settling: a new jar that has settled only 15–20 minutes cannot automatically give final sand/silt/clay percentages. Document its provisional layers and return after the validated settling interval, or compare with a clearly labelled pre-settled reference jar of the same soil without claiming its readings as your own.

Finish the report when actual measurements and the appropriate laboratory reference are available. Give at least two reasoned tomato-oriented actions and an exit-ticket answer naming the single highest priority with evidence. Sentence starters may help drafting; an advanced learner can add a conditional texture or tomato requirement recommendation with supporting reference. sourceBindings.text: The supplied model, not your field result, is 45% sand, 35% silt and 20% clay (loam), pH 6.4, OM 2.1%, P 12 ppm and K 185 ppm. It labels pH and K optimum, P and OM low. Its OM label is unsupported by its own chart because 2.1% is inside the 2–3% gap; the model's other nutrient labels also need a matching laboratory method and crop/regional reference. Keep the source values and expose this limitation rather than copying its label into an actual report.

The model proposes 2–3 inches of compost or rotted manure incorporated into the top 6 inches and a phosphorus-rich product such as bone meal or 10-20-10. Those figures and products are historical classroom examples, not a verified Field 3 prescription. Check material analysis, quality, salinity, nutrient balance, extraction method, crop guidance, environmental risk and lime requirement before specifying any input or rate. Discuss why your own pH/texture can differ from the model and why recommendation quality matters more than matching a model number. A self-reflection checklist helps plan improvement but does not prove practical competence.

The separate tomato model answer also proposes a pH target of at least 6.2, 2–3 inches of compost or well-rotted manure, and bone meal, 10-20-10 or triple superphosphate; it says no additional potassium. These are illustrative model proposals to examine, not verified prescriptions. A final crop target, material choice, incorporation plan and decision to add or withhold K require the actual method-calibrated report, nutrient budget and site evidence. The template places MAP before planting; the tomato answer also mixes its proposed phosphorus product into soil before planting. Retain that example timing only if a qualified local plan supports the material and placement.
